newsitem.title: FRANCE: French centre-right ahead, many voters undecided.
newsitem.headline: French centre-right ahead, many voters undecided.

text.p: France's ruling centre-right coalition remains the narrow favourite to win next month's parliamentary election although close to a third of voters may yet change their minds, an opinion poll showed on Tuesday.

The Louis Harris poll for the magazine Valeurs Actuelles credited the centre-right with 39 percent of the vote, against 38.5 percent for the leftist bloc. The far-right National Front scored 15.5 percent and the Greens seven percent.
Thirty-one percent said they could yet change their minds in the poll which questioned 945 people on Monday.
An IFOP survey for VSD magazine showed voters narrowly favour Socialist Lionel Jospin as prime minister over incumbent Alain Juppe but more than a third are indifferent to the May 25-June 1 election.
But the same survey also showed 39 percent of respondents wanted a victory for the governing centre-right, and 33 percent a leftist win.
The poll found that Jospin was the best prime minister for France according to 37 percent of voters. Thirty-four percent picked Juppe and 21 percent favoured neither.
A CSA poll said that if the centre-right won, 40 percent of voters wanted National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin to replace Juppe.
A Sofres poll for the daily Le Monde found more than a third of voters believed neither the centre-right nor the left would address their concerns.
The poll found that voters had slightly greater confidence in the ruling coalition to run France than in the Socialists, but neither party had the confidence of most French people.
Thirty-five percent supported the centre-right, 32 percent the Socialists and 31 percent had confidence in neither.

Another SOFRES poll for the business weekly L'Usine Nouvelle showed that tax cuts should be the new government's priority for 52 percent of voters, with wage increases to boost consumer demand the next priority for 44 percent.
